title: Medellín: El Poblado and Provenza
summary: From the metro by the river, through old Manila and the square where El Poblado began, to Parque Lleras, the La Octava ball-pit bar and the leafy cafés of Provenza.
intro: Welcome to El Poblado! Today this is Medellín's most international neighbourhood, full of trees, cafés, restaurants and bars. But it's also where the story of the city began, more than four hundred years ago. This walk takes about two hours, starting at the Poblado metro station and climbing gently through the neighbourhood to Provenza. There are plenty of chances to stop for a coffee, a juice or something to eat, so take your time. Keep your phone in your pocket between stops, and let's go.

stops.name: Poblado Metro Station
stops.text: We start at the corner of Poblado station, on Line A of the Medellín Metro. Opened in 1995, it is still the only metro in Colombia, and people here are very proud of it. Notice how clean it is: no graffiti, no litter. Locals call this respect for shared spaces cultura metro, metro culture. Line A runs along the Medellín River, right at the bottom of the valley. From here we walk uphill, east, toward the mountains. Walk east along Calle 10, and cross the big avenues only at the traffic lights.
stops.credit: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Across Avenida Las Vegas
stops.text: At Avenida Las Vegas, cross at the lights, then bear left toward Calle 11. Somewhere under your feet, the La Presidenta stream is finishing its trip down the hill into the river. We'll meet the same stream later, up in a green park.

stops.name: Onto Calle 11
stops.text: Keep going east along Calle 11. The flat valley floor behind you is a tangle of avenues, rails and the river; from here the city starts to climb.

stops.name: Left onto Carrera 43F
stops.text: Turn left onto Carrera 43F, a quiet street of low houses. You're entering Manila.

stops.name: Right onto Calle 11A
stops.text: Turn right onto Calle 11A and walk a few steps.

stops.name: Manila
stops.text: Welcome to Manila, one of the oldest residential corners of El Poblado. Look at the scale of it: two- and three-storey houses, a tight grid of streets, trees, and almost no towers. Many of these old family homes are now cafés, small restaurants, hostels and co-working spaces, which gives the neighbourhood a young, relaxed feel. Nearby there's even a public skate park, busy in the afternoons. It's a good place to see how El Poblado looked before the high-rises arrived. Now keep walking east along Calle 11A.

stops.name: Right onto Carrera 43B
stops.text: At Carrera 43B, turn right and walk downhill, south.

stops.name: Across Calle 10A
stops.text: Cross Calle 10A carefully and keep going straight down Carrera 43B.

stops.name: Milla de Oro
stops.text: One block to your left runs Avenida El Poblado, also called Carrera 43A. For most of the twentieth century this area was countryside: big country houses, called fincas, where wealthy families from downtown came to escape the city. As Medellín grew, the fincas were replaced by apartment towers, hotels and offices, and the stretch of the avenue further south became known as the Milla de Oro, the Golden Mile, for its banks and business headquarters. Cross Calle 10 at the lights; the square with the church is right ahead.

stops.name: El Poblado Park
stops.text: You're standing where Medellín began. In 1616, a Spanish colonial official, Francisco de Herrera Campuzano, set up a settlement for the indigenous people of the valley right here, called San Lorenzo de Aburrá. That's why this neighbourhood is called El Poblado, the settlement. The town of Medellín itself grew up later, further north, where the Centro is today. Look around at the mountains on every side. Medellín sits in a long, narrow valley, at about fifteen hundred metres, and the temperature stays pleasant all year. That's why it's called the City of Eternal Spring.

stops.name: San José del Poblado Church
stops.text: This is the church of San José del Poblado, the parish church of the neighbourhood. Look up at its tall brick tower with the clock. Like in almost every Colombian town, the square and the church go together: for centuries this was where people met after Sunday mass, did business and caught up on news. El Poblado has changed completely around it, but the plaza and its church are still the heart of the old village. If the doors are open, step inside for a quiet moment. Then walk south along Carrera 43A, toward the green park by the stream.
stops.place: Parroquia San José del Poblado Medellín

stops.name: South on Carrera 43A
stops.text: Walk south along the sidewalk of Carrera 43A, Avenida El Poblado, for about two blocks, until Calle 8.

stops.name: Left onto Calle 8
stops.text: Turn left onto Calle 8, away from the traffic.

stops.name: Right onto Carrera 42
stops.text: Turn right onto Carrera 42 and look for the trees and the path by the stream. It's suddenly much quieter here.

stops.name: La Presidenta Linear Park
stops.text: This green strip follows the La Presidenta stream down the hill, the same stream you crossed near the metro. Medellín is crossed by hundreds of streams like this one, all flowing into the river at the bottom of the valley. In recent years the city has been turning streets and streams into green corridors, planting thousands of trees and plants to cool the city down, and it won international awards for it. Listen for the birds. You might see bright green parakeets, or the noisy, yellow-chested bird locals call the bichofué. Now follow the path east, along the stream.
stops.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: To Carrera 39
stops.text: Follow the path along the stream until you reach Carrera 39. Medellín's streams flood fast in heavy rain, which is why many run in deep channels like this one.

stops.name: Left onto Calle 8
stops.text: Walk down Carrera 39 to Calle 8 and turn left, walking east. Look for a bar on this street.

stops.name: La Octava
stops.text: This is La Octava, one of the most famous bars in El Poblado, and a little crazy. Its best-known feature is a ball pit, a piscina de pelotas, like the ones in children's play areas, except this one is for grown-ups, who jump in with a drink in hand. The house shot has a cheeky name: the Russian cocaine. Relax, it's just a drink, and the name is a joke. The bar comes alive at night, so if you like what you see, come back later. And like everywhere in the nightlife zone: drink at your own pace, and never leave your glass alone. Now walk up Carrera 38, toward Parque Lleras.

stops.name: Up Carrera 38
stops.text: Walk up Carrera 38 to Calle 9; the park is right ahead. We're in the Zona Rosa, the nightlife district: calm by day, packed by night. A few honest tips for going out in Medellín. Use ride apps, or taxis that a restaurant or bar calls for you. Don't accept drinks from strangers. And be careful when meeting people from dating apps.

stops.name: Parque Lleras
stops.text: This is Parque Lleras, the heart of El Poblado's nightlife. Around this small, leafy park are dozens of bars, clubs and restaurants, and on weekend nights it fills with locals and travellers from all over the world. Medellín's music is everywhere. The city is often called the capital of reggaetón: stars like J Balvin, Karol G and Maluma all come from Medellín. But you'll also hear salsa, vallenato and electronic music. If you want to learn a few dance steps, many places offer salsa classes for beginners. Now walk up Carrera 38, toward Calle 10.

stops.name: Right onto Calle 10
stops.text: At the top of Carrera 38, turn right onto Calle 10 and walk east. While you walk, let's talk about food. The classic dish of this region is the bandeja paisa, a huge plate with beans, rice, ground beef, crispy pork belly called chicharrón, a fried egg, sweet plantain, avocado, a little arepa and chorizo. It's a farmer's meal, so share it. For something smaller, try an arepa, or an empanada with spicy ají sauce.

stops.name: Provenza
stops.text: Welcome to Provenza, the trendiest corner of Medellín. These leafy streets are full of small boutiques, restaurants, rooftop bars and cafés. Look into the shops and you'll find many Colombian designers. Medellín is a fashion city, built on the textile industry you hear about on the downtown tour, and every July it hosts Colombiamoda, one of the biggest fashion fairs in Latin America. Keep walking east to Carrera 35, the street with the most trees of all.

stops.name: Right onto Carrera 35
stops.text: Turn right onto Carrera 35 and walk down it, under the big trees.

stops.name: Carrera 35
stops.text: This stretch of Carrera 35 is the heart of Provenza: a street shaded by big trees, lined with terraces and restaurants. This is a great place to stop for a while. Colombia is one of the world's great coffee countries, and the mountains around Medellín are coffee country too. Many cafés here serve speciality coffee from small farms; ask where it comes from. Or order a tinto, the small black coffee Colombians drink all day long. And try the fruit juices: lulo is tangy and green inside, maracuyá is passion fruit, guanábana is creamy and sweet.
stops.credit: José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Right onto Calle 8
stops.text: At the bottom of Carrera 35, turn right onto Calle 8.

stops.name: Almost there
stops.text: Follow Calle 8 a few more steps, then turn right into the small park.

stops.name: Parque La 37
stops.text: This quiet little park, Parque La 37, is the end of our walk. In a couple of hours you've gone from the metro by the river, through the old streets of Manila, to the square where El Poblado was born four hundred years ago, and up to the streets where Medellín eats, shops and dances today. If you haven't done it yet, the downtown tour tells the other half of the story: how Medellín went from one of the most dangerous cities in the world to one of the most innovative. Thank you for walking with me. Enjoy your coffee, and enjoy Medellín. Gracias, parce.
